newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - U.S. aid for Bosnian army provokes debate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. aid for Bosnian army provokes debate.

text.p: For the young Bosnian army officer, all hell was breaking loose.
Enemy mortar fire rained down. Shrapnel wounded one of his men in the leg. As he called in reinforcements, a hostile MiG-21 aircraft zoomed overhead.
Captain Adis Ducic's men appeared as blue dots on a television monitor and the "enemy force" was sitting in a room down the corridor, controlling an imaginary army on a computer.
The battle was all in a day's training for 24-year-old Ducic who came to the simulation centre to learn from his American mentors how to wage war.

In a building where Bosnian Serb officers once orchestrated the siege of Sarajevo, retired U.S. officers are teaching tactics as part of a $100 million military aid programme for the country's Moslem-Croat federation army.

The Americans say the "train and equip" programme will create a balance of power by providing a counterweight to the Serb military, which enjoyed vast superiority over the Bosnian army during the 1992-95 war.
European governments fear that arms deliveries and training could lay the ground for another conflict in the Balkans, undermining an expensive effort to build a stable peace.
The Bosnian Serbs are deeply nervous about "train and equip", citing it as an excuse to avoid complying with an arms control agreement for Moslem-Croat and Serb territories.

At the simulation centre, Bosnian officers are using the same computers and software employed by NATO to rehearse for the Gulf War, measuring their decisions against variables such as the effect of humidity on artillery fire.

The extent of U.S. assistance has proved disappointing for some federation commanders. But young Moslem officers such as Ducic say the programme means never having to repeat the terrifying experience of entering a war badly outgunned.
"In 1992, I lost almost all of my friends. The Serbs drove in tanks and we had one anti-tank rocket. We had to decide when we would fire it," Ducic said.
"Now I feel much safer. If they attack us, we won't let them do that again."
FIRST FORMAL MILITARY EDUCATION

Most of the officers in the federation have no formal military education and are learning how to coordinate troop movement and firepower for the first time, something none of the rival armies were able to do consistently during the war.

Although the Americans insist they are training the federation army to act only as a defensive force, officers in the federation say the "command and control" principles being taught can be applied in either direction.
Unlike advisers who served in Vietnam or Central America, the U.S. instructors dress in civilian clothes and are employed by a private firm contracted to manage the programme.

Military Professional Resources Inc. is the same U.S. company that Croatia hired to train its army before launching successful offensives in 1995. The reorganised military went on to recapture Serb-held territory inside Croatia and helped Moslem forces push back the Serbs in northwest Bosnia.

Apart from tanks, artillery, machine-guns and radio equipment supplied by the United States, Islamic countries such as the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia are donating substantial heavy weaponry and funds.

Washington, saying it had discovered a budget surplus, recently sweetened its aid package and announced it would deliver an additional 116 howitzers this year. The UAE sent some 50 French-made MX-30 tanks to the federation this month.
SPECULATION ABOUT NEW WAR
The arms deliveries coincide with speculation in the Sarajevo media that another war will be fought to settle territorial disputes left over from the war.

With Moslem refugees barred from returning to their homes in Serb-controlled territory and Serb leaders obstructing efforts to reunify the country, Balkan analysts say the federation army may be preparing for a possible assault to be launched after the NATO-led peace force eventually departs.
Officers in the NATO-led force say they are carefully monitoring the military balance between the armies as the federation rapidly rebuilds.
"There is a danger that one side crosses the line. That's a concern and we are watching it very closely," a NATO officer said.

The Serbs, backed by their patrons in neighbouring Yugoslavia, still have large numbers of artillery and tanks. But morale is on the decline and they are struggling to maintain weapons and pay officers in a deteriorating economy.
James Pardew, the U.S. diplomat and former colonel overseeing the programme, says nationalist Serb leaders -- not military aid -- are undermining the peace.
"If there's a threat to peace it is a failure of (Serb leaders) to comply with the provisions of the Dayton peace agreement," Pardew said.

The train and equip programme was also devised to placate the U.S. Congress, which saw military aid as a way of ensuring that the federation could defend itself after American peacekeeping troops leave.

But European officers in NATO, who strongly oppose "train and equip", say the United States may have to reconsider withrawing its troops in a year as planned to keep the revitalised federation army from taking action.
Carl Bildt, former international High Representative to Bosnia, said "train and equip" may set off an arms race that would make a U.S.-led peace force more vital than ever.
"Train and equip might create military instability that is going to make it absolutely essential to keep the troops here, which is not the way it was originally designed," Bildt said.
